params.question: In the normal menstrual cycle, which event directly triggers the onset of menstruation?

answers.text: A surge in luteinising hormone at mid-cycle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The LH surge occurs at mid-cycle and triggers ovulation, not menstruation. Ovulation happens approximately fourteen days before the next period begins.

answers.text: Breakdown of the corpus luteum with withdrawal of progesterone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When no pregnancy occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates. The resulting fall in progesterone — which had been stabilising the endometrium — destabilises the lining and triggers shedding.

answers.text: Rising oestradiol levels from the dominant follicle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rising oestradiol is a feature of the follicular phase and drives endometrial proliferation. It does not trigger menstruation.

answers.text: A sharp increase in follicle stimulating hormone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: FSH rises at the start of a new cycle to recruit follicles, but it is the withdrawal of progesterone from the degenerating corpus luteum that initiates menstruation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The trigger for menstruation is the breakdown of the corpus luteum. Without sustained progesterone, the endometrium loses its hormonal support and sheds — this is also why anovulatory cycles produce unpredictable, often heavy bleeding.
Exactly right. The corpus luteum has a limited lifespan; when it breaks down, progesterone withdrawal destabilises the endometrium and triggers menstrual shedding.

params.question: In a woman with previously regular monthly cycles, secondary amenorrhoea is diagnosed only after six months without a period.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The six-month threshold applies only to women with already irregular cycles. For a woman who previously had regular monthly periods, secondary amenorrhoea is diagnosed after three months without a period — a much shorter wait, because missing three consecutive regular cycles is clearly abnormal.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well spotted. For women with previously regular cycles, secondary amenorrhoea is diagnosed after just three months without a period. The six-month threshold applies only to women whose cycles were already irregular, because variable gaps are expected in conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome.

interactions.label: A 54-year-old woman reports a single episode of light vaginal spotting eighteen

params.question: A 54-year-old woman reports a single episode of light vaginal spotting eighteen months after her last period. She feels well and has no other symptoms. What is the most important next step?

answers.text: Reassure and observe, since a single light episode is unlikely to be significant

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Any bleeding after menopause — even a single light episode — must be investigated. The cardinal rule is that postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

answers.text: Arrange a thyroid function test and serum prolactin level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thyroid and prolactin tests are useful in reproductive-age women with menstrual irregularity, but they do not address the key concern in postmenopausal bleeding — excluding endometrial malignancy.

answers.text: Start tranexamic acid and review after three months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Empirical treatment without investigation is dangerous in postmenopausal bleeding. Malignancy must be excluded before any treatment is considered, no matter how light the bleeding.

answers.text: Refer for endometrial sampling to exclude malignancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Postmenopausal bleeding is treated as endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Endometrial sampling should never be delayed, regardless of the amount or frequency of bleeding.

overallFeedback.feedback: In postmenopausal bleeding, ruling out endometrial malignancy takes absolute priority. This principle overrides all other considerations, no matter how light or infrequent the bleeding appears.

Correct. Postmenopausal bleeding — defined as bleeding twelve or more months after the last period — always requires endometrial sampling to exclude malignancy, even when the bleeding appears trivial.

params.question: A 19-year-old girl presents with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche. She bruises easily and had prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. Her mother also reports heavy periods. Which PALM-COEIN category best explains her bleeding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While anovulatory cycles are common in teenagers, the family history of heavy periods and the personal history of easy bruising and prolonged post-procedural bleeding point to a systemic bleeding disorder, not ovulatory dysfunction.

Heavy bleeding since menarche, easy bruising, prolonged post-procedural bleeding, and a positive family history form the classic presentation of an inherited coagulopathy, most commonly von Willebrand disease.
Endometrial polyps are uncommon in teenagers. More importantly, polyps would not explain the systemic bruising tendency or prolonged bleeding after dental extraction.
Primary endometrial disorders can cause heavy menstrual bleeding, but they do not explain the systemic features — easy bruising and prolonged post-procedural bleeding — which indicate a coagulopathy.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is recognising the systemic bleeding features: easy bruising and prolonged post-procedural bleeding are not explained by a local uterine cause. Combined with onset at menarche and a family history, these features strongly suggest AUB-C (coagulopathy), most commonly von Willebrand disease.

Correct. The combination of heavy bleeding from menarche, easy bruising, prolonged post-procedural bleeding, and a family history is the classic picture of an inherited coagulopathy — the 'C' in COEIN — most commonly von Willebrand disease.
